**Research note: PostgreSQL limits for schema and pool sizing**

I read three pages of the official PostgreSQL documentation. A subagent fetched them for me, and I haven't re-read them myself. The pages were the "current" docs, which the fetch reported as PostgreSQL 19.

**Identifier length.** By default an identifier can be at most 63 bytes. The docs say `NAMEDATALEN` is 64 by default, so the maximum identifier length is 63 bytes (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). The limit is counted in bytes, not characters. Names with multi-byte UTF-8 characters, such as accented or CJK letters, therefore have fewer usable characters. Longer names are not rejected. They are silently truncated, so two long names sharing the same first 63 bytes will collide. The limits table says this can be raised by recompiling PostgreSQL (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html), which is impractical on managed services. Keep generated names, such as index and constraint names built from table and column names, comfortably under 63 bytes.

**Columns per table.** The hard limit is 1,600 columns per table. The limits table adds that this is further limited by the tuple having to fit on a single page (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). The docs say the maximum is reduced because the stored row must fit in a single 8192-byte heap page. Their example is that 1,600 `bigint` columns (12,800 bytes) would not fit. In practice, wide tables hit the page-size limit well before 1,600 columns. Large variable-length values can be stored out of line, so the effective ceiling depends on your column types. A new service should be nowhere near this limit, and a table approaching a few hundred columns probably needs normalising.

**Default max_connections.** The default is typically 100 connections, but it might be lower if kernel settings can't support it, as determined during `initdb` (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). The same page notes that a standby server must set this parameter to the same or a higher value than the primary. Otherwise queries are not allowed on the standby. Managed providers often override the default, so check the value on your actual instance with `SHOW max_connections;`.

**Recommendation.** Keep identifiers well under 63 bytes, and keep tables far narrower than 1,600 columns, because the 8 KB page limit bites first. Size the application pool so the total across all service instances stays well below `max_connections` (default 100). Leave headroom for admin, migration and replica connections, and consider a pooler such as PgBouncer if you need more concurrent clients.

{"answers": {"1": "63 bytes (NAMEDATALEN 64 minus 1)", "2": "1,600 columns (further limited by 8192-byte page tuple fit)", "3": "100 (typically; may be lower depending on kernel settings at initdb)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html", "https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html"], "2": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html"]}}

**Research note: PostgreSQL memory and WAL defaults (current docs, v18)**

I checked the three defaults on the official PostgreSQL 18 documentation pages. A subagent fetched and read both pages and quoted the sentences below back to me. I did not open the pages myself. Search results also pointed to third-party pages, but I relied only on the official pages.

**work_mem.** The default is 4MB. The docs say "The default value is four megabytes (4MB)" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-resource.html). This limit applies per sort or hash operation, not per query or per connection. One complex query can use several multiples of it, and many concurrent sessions multiply that again. Raising it globally is risky on a busy server.

**shared_buffers.** The default is typically 128MB. The docs add that it "might be less if your kernel settings will not support it (as determined during initdb)" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-resource.html). So on a fresh install, check the value the server actually reports with `SHOW shared_buffers;` before assuming 128MB. It is a conservative figure meant to start on almost any machine, and it is usually too low for a dedicated database server.

**max_wal_size.** The default is 1GB. The docs say "The default is 1 GB" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-wal.html). It is a soft limit that triggers checkpoints, so WAL can briefly exceed it. A write-heavy workload with this default will checkpoint frequently, which adds I/O spikes.

**Caveats.** I only read the version 18 pages. Older releases may differ, and managed services such as Azure compute some of these values at provisioning time. Check `SHOW` or `pg_settings` on the actual instance.

**Recommendation.** Raise shared_buffers well above 128MB, since the docs' own rule of thumb is about 25% of RAM on a dedicated server with at least 1GB. Increase max_wal_size if the logs show checkpoints happening too often, and leave work_mem near 4MB globally, raising it per session or per role for specific heavy queries.

{"answers": {"1": "4MB", "2": "128MB (typically; may be less if kernel settings don't support it)", "3": "1GB"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-resource.html"], "2": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-resource.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-wal.html"]}}

**Research note: choosing an analytics side-store next to PostgreSQL, and MERGE on PostgreSQL 15**

I looked up three facts for this decision. I did not read the pages myself. A research subagent fetched them and reported the quotes below, so these figures rest on its reading of each page.

**DuckDB memory.** DuckDB's configuration page lists `memory_limit` (alias `max_memory`) with a default of 80% of system RAM (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html). The page gives this only in a table, not in prose. The stable docs URL redirected to a versioned page, and the value was not checked on the current stable docs. If DuckDB shares a host with PostgreSQL, that 80% default can crowd out Postgres's shared buffers and OS cache. Set `memory_limit` explicitly on a shared machine.

**SQLite file size.** The SQLite limits page gives the maximum database file size as approximately 2.8e+14 bytes, or 281 terabytes (256 tebibytes). This assumes the maximum page size of 65536 bytes and the maximum of 4294967294 pages (source: https://sqlite.org/limits.html). Few analytics workloads will hit this ceiling. Practical constraints such as single-writer concurrency and the lack of columnar execution will matter long before it.

**MERGE in PostgreSQL.** The PostgreSQL 15 release notes list "Support for the SQL MERGE command" among the new features. The Utility Commands section says the command was added "to adjust one table to match another" and is "similar to INSERT ... ON CONFLICT but more batch-oriented" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/release-15.html). So PostgreSQL 15 is the first major version with MERGE, and you can use it on 15. The current MERGE reference page (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-merge.html) does not state the introducing version, so I did not rely on it for that point.

**Recommendation.** Choose DuckDB as the analytics side-store, because it is columnar and built for analytical queries over data exported from or attached to PostgreSQL. SQLite's file-size limit is not a concern, but it is a row-oriented transactional engine. Cap DuckDB's memory if it shares a host with PostgreSQL. MERGE is available on PostgreSQL 15, so you can use it for upserts and syncs.

{"answers": {"1": "80% of RAM", "2": "about 281 TB (2.8e+14 bytes; 256 TiB)", "3": "PostgreSQL 15"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html"], "2": ["https://sqlite.org/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/release-15.html"]}}

**Research note: TLS version, DNS label length and HTTP 418**

**TLS 1.3.** TLS 1.3 is specified by RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3", a Standards Track document from August 2018. Its abstract says "This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol." (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446.txt)

**DNS label length.** A single label, meaning one dot-separated component of a host name, can be at most 63 octets. RFC 1035 section 2.3.4 lists "labels 63 octets or less" and "names 255 octets or less". Section 3.1 explains the label limit: the length field leaves only six bits for the length. (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035.txt) The 255-octet limit applies to the whole name. It is measured in the wire format, so the usable text length of a dotted name is slightly shorter.

**HTTP 418.** Status code 418 is "I'm a teapot". RFC 2324 defines it in section 2.3.2: "Any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code '418 I'm a teapot'." That RFC is the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0), an Informational document dated 1 April 1998. (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324.txt)

The current HTTP semantics specification, RFC 9110, lists 418 as "(Unused)" in section 15.5.19. It says the code is reserved in the IANA registry because it was "deployed as a joke often enough for the code to be unusable for any future use". (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt) So 418 is a real, reserved code with a defined origin, but it is a joke and not part of the working HTTP vocabulary.

**Caveat on how I read these.** The fetch tool summarised each page, so the quotes come from that summary. I did not read the raw text myself. The RFC numbers and limits are standard and match what I'd expect, but check the quotes against the RFCs before citing them verbatim in the guideline.

**Recommendation.** Require TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) as the baseline, and keep host-name checks to 63 octets per label and 255 octets per full name (RFC 1035). Don't use 418 for real application errors. RFC 9110 reserves it, so list it as reserved in the guideline.

{"answers": {"1": "RFC 8446", "2": "63 octets", "3": "418; RFC 2324 (reserved/unused in RFC 9110)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446.txt"], "2": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035.txt"], "3": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324.txt", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt"]}}

cd /tmp/research_synthesis_y93rda4b; curl -sL https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446.txt | head -30 | grep -i -E "RFC 8446|TLS|Version 1.3"; echo ==; curl -sL https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035.txt | grep -n -i "63 octets"; echo ==; curl -sL https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324.txt | grep -n "418"; echo ==; curl -sL https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt | grep -n -i "teapot"

**Research note: platform limits for the deploy runbook**

**Lambda timeout.** The AWS Lambda timeout page says you can set the timeout "in increments of 1 second up to a maximum value of 1,800 seconds (30 minutes)" (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). I did not expect this, because the older figure was 900 seconds (15 minutes). The page also mentions a 5,400-second (90-minute) allowance for asynchronous invocations and event source mappings on functions using Lambda Managed Instances. I read that as an exception that doesn't apply to ordinary functions. Please check your account and region against the page before you hard-code 1,800.

**Kubernetes grace period.** A Pod's default termination grace period is 30 seconds. The Pod Lifecycle page says a Pod "is granted a term to terminate gracefully, which defaults to 30 seconds" (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/). The Pod API reference says the same for `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`: "Defaults to 30 seconds" (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1/). The fetch tool only partly read both pages and gave me those quotes from a summary of the unread part. The 30-second figure is consistent across both, but I did not see the verbatim text.

**Docker docker0 subnet.** Mirantis' documentation states that "the default IP range, or subnet, for `docker0` is `172.17.0.0/16`" (source: https://docs.mirantis.com/mke/3.7/install/plan-deployment/mcr-considerations/docker0.html). Mirantis is a third party, and the fetch tool returned this sentence from a summary of the unread part of the page. Docker's own pages do not state the figure outright. The bridge driver page shows default-bridge containers at 172.17.0.2 and 172.17.0.3 (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/). The networking overview lists 172.17.0.0/16 as the first built-in address pool (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/). Those are consistent with the Mirantis statement but are not an explicit docker0 default. Docker can pick a different range if 172.17.0.0/16 conflicts with the host network, so local setups may differ.

**Recommendation.** Set the service's graceful-shutdown logic to finish well inside 30 seconds, or raise `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` explicitly. Treat the Lambda timeout as the hard ceiling for one invocation, confirm the 1,800-second figure in your own account, and don't assume 172.17.0.0/16 on developer machines that use VPNs or corporate ranges.

{"answers": {"1": "1,800 seconds (30 minutes)", "2": "30 seconds", "3": "172.17.0.0/16"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html"], "2": ["https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/", "https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1/"], "3": ["https://docs.mirantis.com/mke/3.7/install/plan-deployment/mcr-considerations/docker0.html"]}}

**Research note: test and tooling defaults**

**Vitest per-test timeout.** The default `testTimeout` is 5,000 ms in Node.js. It rises to 15,000 ms when `browser.enabled` is true. Setting it to `0` disables the timeout completely (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout). If the repo only runs Node tests, 5 s is the number to remember. A browser-mode project gets 15 s without any extra config.

**First kernel with Rust.** Linux 6.1, released 11 December 2022, is the release that added Rust support. The kernelnewbies page for that release says: "This release adds support for the Rust programming language." (source: https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1). That page does not say outright that 6.1 was the first kernel to include Rust. I read it as the first because it is the release that adds Rust support. The search results agreed, but I did not open those pages. The support in 6.1 was deliberately minimal, so 6.1 is the floor for "has Rust at all" and not a practical target for real Rust kernel work.

**PostgreSQL `statement_timeout`.** The default is 0, which disables the timeout. The PostgreSQL documentation says: "A value of zero (the default) disables the timeout." A value given without units is read as milliseconds (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). The page I read was the current documentation, which is labelled PostgreSQL 19. Out of the box, no query is ever cut off by the server, so any limit has to be set deliberately.

**Recommendation.** Set the vitest `testTimeout` explicitly in the shared config instead of relying on the 5 s default, especially if any project switches to browser mode. Set a nonzero `statement_timeout` per role or database, since the server default never times out. For the kernel, pin the team's baseline to a recent release, because 6.1 only marks when Rust first appeared.

{"answers": {"1": "5000 ms (15000 ms when browser.enabled)", "2": "Linux 6.1", "3": "0 (disabled, no timeout)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout"], "2": ["https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html"]}}
